evals.prompt: I'm organizing KestrelConf, a 2-day developer conference in Lisbon, about 1,100 attendees, 4th edition, tickets sold to individuals mostly across Europe plus some from the US. We've done a lot this year: banned single-use plastic, switched to reusable lanyards, bought 400 tonnes of certified offsets through a broker, and lunch is 50% vegetarian. Marketing wants a sustainability page live before early-bird closes in 3 weeks. Can you write the page? We want to call it a carbon-neutral conference since the offsets cover more than our estimate. Our estimate came from a 'typical attendee = 350 kg' rule of thumb a sponsor gave us.
evals.expected_output: A pre-event sustainability page draft that refuses carbon-neutral wording under the EU rule, rebuilds the figure as a cited, labelled range led by travel, demotes plastic and lanyards to this edition's actions, keeps the offset purchase on its own contribution line, and flags a jurisdiction review.
expectations: Refuses to describe the event as carbon neutral, climate neutral or CO2 compensated anywhere in the page draft

States that claiming neutral, reduced or positive greenhouse-gas impact on the basis of offsetting is a blacklisted commercial practice in the EU under Directive (EU) 2024/825, applying since 27 September 2026, and that a conference ticket sold to individuals falls in scope
States that the ban applies whatever the quality of the credits bought
Uses no generic label such as eco-friendly, green conference, zero impact, or sustainable as a bare label, and proposes no home-made badge

Rejects the sponsor's 350 kg per attendee rule of thumb as an uncited factor and tells the user to pull a named public factor set (UK DESNZ, ICAO calculator or ADEME Base Empreinte), recording set, edition year and unit
Presents the footprint as a low-to-high range, never a single point total
Names travel as the dominant line in the page's where-it-comes-from section instead of leading with plastic or lanyards
Places the plastic ban and reusable lanyards under this edition's actions and never as the page headline
Keeps measured emissions, reduction actions and the offset purchase on three separate lines, with the contribution never in the same sentence as the footprint total
Writes the contribution as money given to a named project followed by a statement that it does not cancel the event's emissions
Includes a 'What we do not claim' section stating the event is not called carbon neutral
Flags that this is not legal advice and recommends a qualified review for the EU jurisdiction before the page goes live
States the radiative-forcing choice for flights on the page and labels each line measured, surveyed or estimated
Uses the pre-event page variant: labels the figure as an estimate for this edition and says which lines will be measured from this edition on
Offers the page section by section for validation rather than delivering one final block

evals.prompt: We run Tanager Summit, a 3-day infrastructure conference in Singapore, 5th edition, around 1,800 people. Last year's registrations: 35% Singapore and Malaysia, 20% rest of Asia-Pacific, 25% Europe, 15% North America, 5% other. Format is in-person only (decided), venue is signed through 2028. Registration opens in 6 weeks. The sustainability work is just me, maybe 5 hours a month, no budget. I've drafted the plan: 1) no swag bags, 2) compostable cups, 3) digital-only badges, 4) 'zero waste' as our headline. Please turn that into a proper sustainability plan I can publish.
evals.expected_output: A plan that opens with the closed-and-open list, builds a screening estimate and concentration line, picks the long-haul profile, ranks carbon levers by efficiency down to the 5-hour ceiling, parks the swag and cup items as waste rungs off the headline, and asks for a plan choice before any public text.
expectations: Opens with a closed-and-open list naming the signed venue and the closed in-person format as closed items whose levers move to next edition
Builds a screening estimate from origin buckets, mode shares and named factor placeholders before ranking any lever
Writes the concentration line in the form 'Long-haul flyers are N% of participants and M% of travel emissions' derived from the given origin split
Identifies the long-haul profile (long-haul flyers above about 60% of the travel line) and says the cut-off is self-set
Ranks levers by the long-haul efficiency line with organizer-booked travel policy first and remote speaking option second, stating the ranking explicitly
Deletes the host-city rung for this edition because the venue is signed, and carries it to the next edition
Deletes the remote attendance tier because the format is closed as in-person, and moves the remote speaking option up
Places no swag bags, compostable cups and digital badges as waste rungs outside the carbon ranking, run alongside carbon rungs and never as the headline
Rejects 'zero waste' as the headline and states that swag carbon is small, sits in textiles rather than badges, and that no measured carbon reduction from a swag policy exists in the published record
Cuts the default rung at the stated effort ceiling (about 5 hours a month, no budget) and lists structural rungs as next-edition commitments

Names cadence and the regional hub as what the efficiency order starves, with the condition that promotes each (recurring event with long-haul dominance and community acceptance of a gap year; a strong second cluster with a partner team)
Presents two or three lever plans with trade-offs and one recommendation, and asks for the user's choice before drafting the public page
Schedules origin and mode fields into the registration form before it opens in 6 weeks: departure city or distance band, planned main travel mode, nights, required with a prefer-not-to-say option
Counts speakers, volunteers, organizers and sponsor staff as their own rows in the screening estimate
Asks whether sponsors already bought swag bags or lanyards and routes that cut to event-sponsor-pricing if they did

evals.prompt: Oakmere Data Days, 2nd edition, about 900 attendees, held in Frankfurt. Last year's billing countries: 30% Germany, 25% rest of EU, 20% US, 15% India, 10% rest of world. Venue is unsigned for the next edition, in-person format is fixed. My co-organizer is convinced moving the conference to Amsterdam is the single biggest carbon win because of the rail hub, and wants me to run the numbers to prove it. Can you do the analysis and tell us what the move saves?
evals.expected_output: An analysis that places the audience centre first, finds Frankfurt already central with a dispersed intercontinental audience, sizes a relocation at about a tenth with labelled precedents, ranks remote speaking, travel policy and cadence above the move, keeps the host-city rung open only until the venue signs, and hands venue criteria to the venue-sourcing sibling.
expectations: Builds the screening estimate and writes the concentration line before judging the relocation
Places the audience centre from the origin buckets and states that Frankfurt already sits near the European centre, so the off-centre override does not apply

States that with a dispersed intercontinental audience and a well-placed city, the best alternative city saves about a tenth, citing the modelled AGU 2019 precedent where San Francisco came out about 11% above the footprint-minimising city
Identifies the long-haul profile from the US, India and rest-of-world share and ranks remote speaking option, organizer-booked travel policy and cadence above host-city relocation on value
Does not fabricate a tonnage saved by the Amsterdam move; gives a range with named factor placeholders
States that train versus coach among land travellers is of marginal relevance and that replacing flights is what counts
Keeps the host-city rung live only because the venue is unsigned, and says it closes for this edition when the venue signs
Hands venue criteria (rail access, metered energy data, waste-stream reporting) to event-venue-sourcing instead of picking Amsterdam or Frankfurt
Routes a cadence change (biennial, or alternating in-person and online) to event-format-selection and event-budget instead of deciding it
States that the modelled cut above 90% came from central location plus biennial cadence plus virtual presentations combined, so the combination rather than the city does the work
Presents two or three lever plans with trade-offs and one recommendation
Warns that the 57% versus 67% Leiden and Lyon figures compare a stated intention with an observed share at two specific meetings and must not be used to judge Amsterdam
Labels every cited figure modelled or surveyed

evals.prompt: RiverforkJS is a 1,200-person JavaScript conference in Toronto, 6th edition. About 40% fly in from the US, 15% from Europe and Asia, the rest are Canadian. Our board agreed at the last meeting that going fully hybrid next year is how we fix our carbon footprint: a $49 remote ticket, everything streamed. I'm the sustainability lead. Can you confirm the carbon saving and design the remote tier: platform, pricing, and how we nudge the European and Asian attendees to pick remote?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to decide format for carbon alone, routes the hybrid call to the format-selection sibling with the footprint delta of each option, cites the poor engagement and cost evidence for hybrid, declines to design the remote tier or steer regions to it, and offers the remote speaking option and cadence as higher-ranked alternatives.
expectations: Declines to confirm hybrid as the fix and routes the format decision to event-format-selection, handing it the footprint delta of each option
States that format is never decided for carbon alone

Cites that remote engagement and cost evidence is poor: one major computing conference lost money on full hybrid in 2022 and dropped remote attendance, and another stopped hosting hybrid conferences for lack of attendee participation
Refuses to design the remote tier's platform and pricing, routing remote-side design to hybrid-event-design
Refuses to steer European and Asian attendees to the remote tier, stating the remote option is offered and never used to steer one region
Offers the remote speaking option as the narrower version: offered never imposed, same slot length, same billing
Labels the published figures it cites (fully virtual about 94%, carefully selected hubs about two-thirds) as modelled
Does not apply the rail-profile levers (train-times page, rail deal) to a North American audience with no practical rail option
Builds the screening estimate and the concentration line before discussing any lever
Names cadence (biennial, or alternating in-person and online years) as a higher-value alternative, modelling both stable and pent-up attendance
Records the cost of any hybrid or AV lever for event-budget
Does not fabricate a percent saving for this event's hybrid switch; gives a labelled range or a named placeholder
Treats the board's hybrid decision as an input to event-format-selection rather than as a closed carbon decision

evals.prompt: Pelton Cloud Days just wrapped (3rd edition, 700 attendees, Manchester). I have: venue electricity 18,400 kWh metered, 2,100 meals served, 310 kg food waste weighed, 95 kg donated, 1.2 t general waste. We forgot to ask about travel at registration, but we have billing countries for everyone, and a post-event survey went to 120 people of whom 64 answered with their travel mode. Last year we reported 41 t (that one included travel from a registration question we had back then) using the older edition of the government factors; this year I want the newest edition. Write the public report. I want the headline 'Pelton Cloud Days 2026: 9.8 tonnes CO2e, down 76% on last year' based on venue, food and waste.
evals.expected_output: A post-event report that refuses the travel-free headline and the cross-boundary comparison, rebuilds travel as an estimated band from billing countries with widened range, restates last edition on the new factor basis before any comparison, and fills the 9-category table with labels, owners and ranges.
expectations: Refuses the 9.8 t headline because it omits travel, stating that a total without the dominant line misleads by omission
Uses billing country as a coarse origin proxy, labels the travel line estimated, and widens the range because origin and mode coverage (64 of 700) sits below the 80% threshold
Refuses the 'down 76%' comparison because the boundary changed between editions and must be restated on the same boundary before comparing
Flags that changing the factor-set edition requires restating last edition on the new basis, noting air factors can move 15-40% between editions
Keeps the radiative-forcing choice consistent with last edition, or restates the baseline if it changes
Produces the report as the 9-category table with In/out, activity data, factor (set, edition), low, high, quality and owner columns
Labels venue kWh, meals served and waste weights as measured, the 64 survey answers as surveyed, and travel as estimated
Reports totals and per-attendee figures as ranges, with per attendee-day only as a secondary line
Includes the concentration line: long-haul share of participants and of travel
Includes a screening-estimate-versus-result line with the main reason for the gap, or states that no screening estimate existed
Reports data coverage as the share of registrants with origin and mode
Reports the 310 kg food waste and 95 kg donated as weights, not as CO2 avoided
Lists as a next-edition commitment that origin and mode fields go into the registration form before it opens
Types no factor value from memory; leaves named placeholders (set, edition, unit) for the user to fill from the current DESNZ edition
Names an owner per line, noting the venue operator also reports the venue energy

evals.prompt: Cindermoor DevCon, Berlin, 800 people. We fly in about 25 speakers and fund 12 travel grants for underrepresented developers, mostly from outside Europe. The team proposed three things to cut our footprint: score CFP submissions with a distance penalty so closer speakers rank higher; replace the travel grants with free remote tickets for grantees; and book all speaker flights economy with no exceptions. Write this up as our speaker travel policy.
evals.expected_output: A speaker travel policy that rejects ranking speakers by footprint and the grant replacement, keeps grant trips counted in the inventory, writes the organizer-booked travel policy with its access exceptions, offers remote speaking on equal terms, and counts employer-paid speaker flights once.
expectations: Refuses to rank speakers or CFP submissions by flight footprint or distance, and says so in the plan
Refuses to replace travel grants with remote tickets: travel grants and access commitments win over any lever, and remote speaking is never offered in place of a travel grant
Keeps grant trips in the inventory: trips the event pays for belong to the organizer, are counted, and are never dropped to improve the total

Writes the organizer-booked travel policy as economy by default, direct flights where available, rail under a set journey time, regional keynotes where the programme allows, and a remote keynote option

Adds access exceptions (premium cabin, direct flight, or a flight where the rail journey is too long for the person) owned by event-accessibility-inclusion that override the policy, rejecting 'no exceptions'
States that business and first cabins carry several times the economy factor, premium economy sits close to economy, and connecting itineraries add distance plus an extra take-off and landing
Records cabin class and direct-versus-connecting for every organizer-booked trip in the screening worksheet
Offers remote speaking as an option that is never imposed, with the same slot length and same billing on the schedule
Counts speaker flights paid by employers in the event inventory, notes the employer's Scope 3 also holds them, and states the reduction is never claimed twice
Gives speakers and grant recipients their own rows in the screening estimate, noting speakers often fly further
Places organizer-booked travel policy at the top of the efficiency line and explains it covers the only travel the organizer fully controls
Names remote speaking as the narrowest remote version: one slot, no full remote audience to serve

evals.prompt: Brightwater Labs runs Saltmarsh API Days in San Jose, 1,500 attendees: about 85% from the US West Coast and mountain states, 10% from Canada, 5% from Europe. Our venue told us they're 100% renewable powered through renewable energy credits. Leadership wants the sustainability page to say three things: 'ISO 20121 compliant', 'Net zero by 2030', and 'Powered by 100% renewable energy'. We've read the ISO standard and we have a sustainability policy document. Write the page.
evals.expected_output: A page that drops all three claims as worded: ISO 20121 is a management-system standard requiring a named certifier or a running self-declared cycle, the 2030 target needs a verified plan so action commitments replace it, and certificate-backed power is market-based accounting reported after the location-based figure. Picks the domestic-flying profile and flags US and California rules.
expectations: States that ISO 20121 is an event sustainability management-system standard, not a carbon method, and does not certify a footprint

Allows 'certified to ISO 20121' only with a named certification body, 'self-declared conformity' only if the cycle runs (written policy, issue evaluation, supplier requirements, post-event review), and otherwise says nothing about ISO 20121
Rejects 'ISO 20121 compliant' as worded, since a policy document alone does not run the management-system cycle
Refuses 'Net zero by 2030' on the page: a future target needs a detailed, realistic plan verified by an independent expert; keeps numeric targets internal and publishes action commitments instead
Flags California's AB 1305 website disclosure duties for net zero, carbon neutral or significant-reduction claims by an entity operating in California
Names the FTC Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260) as the US guidance for environmental claims
Separates a renewable supply contract tied to generation from unbundled certificates, and states that '100% renewable powered' via credits is market-based accounting, not a physical change
Reports the location-based venue energy figure first, with the market-based figure only alongside it
Identifies the domestic-flying profile for the mostly-US audience and deletes the train-times page and rail deal
Ranks the domestic efficiency line with organizer-booked travel policy first, remote speaking option second, plant-based default third, venue energy ask fourth
Writes the page with the template's six sections: our footprint, where it comes from, what we change this edition, what we will change next edition, how you can help, what we do not claim
Flags that this is not legal advice and suggests a qualified review for the US and California jurisdiction
Uses no generic label and no carbon-neutral wording
Leaves named placeholders for a cited factor set and states the radiative-forcing choice for flights

evals.prompt: Larkspur Go Meetup, Lyon, monthly, 120 to 150 people, everyone comes by metro, bike or on foot, 2 hours on a weekday evening in a coworking space, pizza and beer paid by a local company. A member asked us to publish our carbon footprint and do 'the usual stuff': a train-times page, a rail partnership, and offsets. I have 2 hours total to spend on this. What should we do and what can we say?
evals.expected_output: A plan that inverts the default: travel is small for a transit audience so food and venue energy lead, rail levers are deleted as moving nobody, offsets are kept out of any neutrality claim, the plant-based default and venue kWh ask fit the 2-hour ceiling, and the page avoids generic labels.
expectations: States that with an audience arriving by transit, travel shrinks and food and venue energy become the main lines
Deletes the train-times page and rail deal as moving nobody: they shift only flyers who have a rail option
Declines offsets as a route to any neutrality claim; any contribution is reported as money given, not tonnes cancelled
Moves the plant-based default and venue energy ask up the ranking, and routes the plant-based default into the catering ask rather than writing the menu
Keeps travel in the boundary with a labelled estimate even though it is small, stating travel is never out
Fits the plan to the 2-hour effort ceiling, naming which rungs fit now and which become next-edition commitments
Adds the food-waste weigh-and-donate rung with its guard: confirm the venue or caterer allows donation and local food-safety rules permit it
Names ADEME Base Empreinte as the factor set to use for an event in France, with set, edition and unit recorded, and types no factor from memory
Gives the footprint as a range with measured, surveyed or estimated labels and a per-attendee figure
Writes page wording with no 'green meetup', 'eco-friendly' or carbon-neutral label, and includes a 'What we do not claim' section
Schedules data capture: meals served, venue kWh for the evening or a venue estimate, and waste weight
Sets the 9-category boundary with a reason per category, marking local transportation, freight and digital in or out explicitly

evals.prompt: Greyfell Observability Summit, Edinburgh, 2 days, 600 attendees, mostly UK and Ireland, about 15% from mainland Europe, a handful from the US. Our finance lead set aside GBP 8,000 to 'go carbon neutral'. Help me pick the best offset projects to cover 100% of the footprint so we can put a carbon-neutral badge on the site. Also, should we go for cheaper avoidance credits so the money covers more tonnes?
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses the badge and the 100%-coverage framing under UK rules, reframes the money as a contribution sized by a published rule, sets integrity, type, registry and retirement requirements if credits are bought, keeps the line apart from the total, and puts reduction levers first.
expectations: Refuses to help reach a carbon-neutral claim through offsets, citing the UK CMA Green Claims Code's requirement to say how far emissions were reduced versus offset and the ASA's position against unqualified carbon-neutral claims
Notes the CMA can fine directly since April 2025
Rejects the carbon-neutral badge as banned or high-risk wording and proposes no home-made label
Recommends contribution framing: funding reported as money given to a named project, not tonnes cancelled

If credits are bought, requires those meeting a recognized integrity benchmark (ICVCM Core Carbon Principles), stating whether they are removals or avoided emissions, and naming the registry and retirement
Answers the avoidance-versus-removal question by requiring the type be stated on the page, rather than choosing cheaper credits to cover more tonnes
Sets the contribution amount by a stated, published rule such as an internal price per estimated tonne, not by 100% coverage
Keeps the GBP 8,000 line apart from the footprint total: never netted against it and never in the same sentence
Writes beside the contribution that it does not cancel the event's emissions

Cites the 2022 football World Cup precedent: a Swiss advertising watchdog upheld all complaints against the carbon-neutral claim, and the offsets covered less than a third of the organizer's own estimate
Routes the GBP 8,000 to event-budget as a climate-contribution cost line
Requires a screening estimate with cited factors and a range before the contribution is sized
Identifies the rail profile for the mostly UK and Ireland audience and ranks the train-times page first on efficiency, ahead of the plant-based default and organizer-booked travel policy
Lists reduction levers before any contribution, both in the plan and on the page

evals.prompt: I organize Thornwick Rust Days in Zurich, 1st edition, expecting about 500 attendees, 30 speakers, 25 volunteers and 20 sponsor staff. Best guess at origins: 40% Switzerland, 30% Germany, Austria, France and Italy, 20% rest of Europe, 10% US and Asia. I found a figure online: 0.25 kg CO2 per passenger-km for flights, and I'll add 10% to all distances for detours. Give me the total footprint as one number I can put in the sponsor deck next week.
evals.expected_output: A screening worksheet that refuses the uncited factor and the home-made distance uplift, returns a labelled low-high range with named factor placeholders, buckets origins with mode shares, adds speaker, volunteer, sponsor-staff and accommodation rows, writes the concentration line, and picks the profile from it.
expectations: Refuses the 0.25 kg per passenger-km figure as uncited and names UK DESNZ, the ICAO calculator or ADEME Base Empreinte as the set to pull, recording set, edition year and unit
Rejects the user's own 10% distance uplift, stating the set's own distance convention applies and no uplift is added on top
Gives the result as a low-to-high range, never one number, and explains the spread from origin assumptions and factor choice, citing that two estimates of the same 2019 meeting differ by about 60%
Builds origin buckets as local, same country, rail-reachable neighbours, rest of continent and intercontinental, with low and high mode shares per bucket
Adds separate rows for speakers, volunteers, organizers and sponsor staff
Adds an accommodation line computed as non-local participants times nights with a hotel-night factor placeholder
States the radiative-forcing choice for flights, names the 1.7 multiplier used by DESNZ, and recommends including it
Uses one factor set for the whole inventory, noting different sets can differ by up to about 5x for the same flight
Writes the concentration line in the form 'Long-haul flyers are N% of participants and M% of travel emissions'
Labels every line estimated for a first edition with no registration data, and states travel stays an estimate band until origin and mode coverage reaches about 80%
Reports the per-attendee intensity alongside the total
Marks any line it cannot estimate as not estimated with a reason, never filling it with a silent fallback factor
States which profile the concentration line picks, showing both the long-haul and the rail plan if the long-haul share of travel sits in the 40-60% band
Schedules the registration fields (departure city or distance band, planned mode, nights) before the form opens

evals.prompt: Our finance and ESG team at Marrowgate (we run Marrowgate Connect, our 2,000-person customer conference in Chicago) wants the event inventory to fit the corporate GHG report. Their instructions to me: exclude speaker flights because their employers pay, exclude sponsor staff travel because that's the sponsors' problem, exclude venue electricity because it's the venue's Scope 2 and not ours, include only what we pay for, and structure everything as Scope 1, 2 and 3. Set up the boundary that way.
evals.expected_output: A boundary built on the 9 event categories with one owner per line, keeping every participant travel line in, counting employer-paid speaker flights and sponsor-staff travel with co-reporters named, reporting venue energy with the venue noted as co-reporter, and offering the Scope 1/2/3 mapping only as a separate corporate view.
expectations: Keeps attendee, speaker, volunteer and sponsor-staff travel in the event inventory, stating travel is never out
Uses the 9 Net Zero Carbon Events categories for the event inventory and maps to Scope 1, 2 and 3 only as a separate view for the corporate report
States that attendee travel and accommodation sit in the organizer's Scope 3, and that venue electricity is Scope 2 only when the organizer controls the venue
Counts speaker flights paid by employers in the event inventory, notes the employer's Scope 3 also holds them, and states the reduction is never claimed twice
Counts sponsor staff travel by default because they travel for the event, and names the sponsor as co-reporter
Reports venue energy in the event inventory and notes the venue operator also reports it
Marks sponsor booth freight as optional: counted if material, otherwise listed as excluded
Names one owner per line in the boundary table
States the common exclusions openly: venue embodied carbon, water, and the organizers' year-round office
Notes that food attendees buy themselves at venue cafes is excluded in the method's first edition
Lists invited-speaker trips and travel grants the organizer pays as owned outright, counted, and never dropped to improve the total
Flags that an 'only what we pay for' boundary omits the dominant line and would mislead on any public page
Distinguishes the event inventory from the company's own business-travel inventory and does not build the latter
Flags renewable certificates bought by the venue: report the location-based figure first, market-based only alongside it
